title: 10,500-year-old wooden posts found beneath german lake
dek: Divers recovered split boards and a tall post from lake arendsee, where waterlogged conditions have preserved stone-age timbers rarely seen elsewhere.
body: Archaeologists exploring lake arendsee in northern germany have recovered remarkably well-preserved pieces of worked wood dating back as much as 10,500 years. The finds were made during underwater investigations by the State Office for Heritage Management and Archaeology of Saxony-Anhalt, researchers have identified wooden posts and split boards bearing evidence of human workmanship beneath approximately 20 metres of water. Whether the timbers represent the remains of dwellings or another type of wooden structure is not yet known, and archaeologists emphasise that investigations are continuing.

The discovery is particularly significant because wooden objects from the mesolithic, or middle stone age, have only rarely survived. Besides the usual finds from this period, such as stone tools or animal bones, divers were able to recover spectacular pieces of wood, which have very rarely survived from this era. The finds shed a completely new light on the mesolithic period, for which traces of buildings in central germany have so far only been known in the form of soil discolourations.

Among the discoveries is a post measuring approximately 1.6 metres in height that bears apparent felling marks. Researchers have also recovered split boards measuring up to 1.3 metres long. Initial investigations suggest that the pieces could have belonged to structures constructed by people living around lake arendsee approximately 10,500 years ago. At the time, communities in the region lived by hunting, gathering and fishing rather than agriculture.

Project manager marcel weiss said determining exactly what the wooden remains represent could have important implications for archaeologists’ understanding of mesolithic communities. Whether we are looking at the remains of huts or other, previously completely unknown wooden structures is the subject of ongoing and future research. If evidence ultimately demonstrates that permanent structures or intensively used living areas existed at lake arendsee 10,500 years ago, it could affect current interpretations of hunter-gatherer societies and the development of cultural landscapes.

Such structures would pre-date the arrival of the first farming communities and their longhouses in central europe by around 3,000 years. The exceptional survival of the wood is linked to the unusual geology of lake arendsee in saxony-anhalt’s altmarkkreis salzwedel district. Unlike many inland lakes, where sediment gradually accumulates and shorelines change through silting, the bottom of lake arendsee has been slowly subsiding as a result of geological processes associated with an underlying salt dome. This process has helped preserve parts of the ancient shoreline and archaeological material beneath a relatively thin layer of sediment.

Lake arendsee has been the subject of underwater archaeological investigations for several years and has already produced finds from several periods. Previous discoveries include neolithic fish weirs, a high medieval flat-bottomed cargo vessel and a late medieval dugout canoe. The latest finds push the archaeological record beneath the lake considerably further back in time and could provide unusually direct evidence of how mesolithic communities worked with wood. Researchers are now attempting to establish whether the posts and boards formed part of huts, another type of construction or something not previously identified in the archaeological record.

For archaeologists, the answer could provide a rare glimpse of structures built by hunter-gatherers more than 10 millennia ago, structures that survived beneath lake arendsee while most comparable traces on land disappeared.
